title: cmuratori-discussion/cleancodeqa.md at main · unclebob/cmuratori-discussion
summary: Muratori and Martin converge: clean-code structures do cost cycles, most business software can afford them, Clean Code teaching neglected performance, tests should be selective, and OO versus switch is a symmetric trade-off.

assertions.quote: It is economically better for most organizations to conserve programmer cycles than computer cycles.

verdicts.note: Much business software is not CPU-bound and developer salaries dominate costs, but published latency experiments show slowness has measurable revenue costs too.

Readability correlated with defect reports, version churn, bug-fix commits and project maturity, and a readability drop in jUnit coincided with rising defect density, supporting that readability relates to quality; correlational and silent on the CPU-vs-programmer-time trade-off.

assertions.quote: Indeed, using those structures can cost you a lot of nanoseconds. They are not efficient at the nanosecond level.
Cycle-lean code can increase efficiency by an order of magnitude; but the right choice of algorithm can increase efficiency by many orders of magnitude.

verdicts.note: Asymptotic improvements dominate constant-factor ones on large inputs, though for fixed-size hot loops constant factors are all that remain.

assertions.quote: not a single one of the things you mentioned here are discussed in the nine hour runtime

verdicts.note: The author conceded the point about his own lecture series; whether audiences actually absorb a disregard for performance is not measured.

assertions.quote: When I have a suite of tests that I trust, and that has high coverage, I can refactor that code without fear.
tests that you don't use, or that don't find bugs, or that took longer to write and maintain than the number of bugs they prevented
I cannot practically write tests for things that I have to see in order to know that they work. GUIs, Game behaviors, Hardware interactions, etc.

verdicts.note: Both debaters and the game industry agree; snapshot and replay testing cover regressions but not the initial judgement of correctness.

assertions.quote: OO (Operand Primal) is a great way to add types to existing functions without changing those functions.

verdicts.note: This is the well-known expression problem; the two designs are mirror images for the two kinds of extension.

assertions.quote: it prevents changes at to low level modules from forcing a wave of recompilation and redeployment from sweeping through the system towards higher level modules

verdicts.note: The mechanism is real, but link-time binding through opaque pointers gives the same isolation, so the benefit specific to runtime polymorphism is mainly plugins and frameworks.

assertions.quote: the idea of structuring code around swappable types is generally wrong
